market.title: IRE condemns post by President Trump depicting violence against journalists

The video, posted on Truth Social, undermines the role of the press in a functioning democracy. It makes light of the violence that many journalists face while…
market.content_text: Nov 10, 2026 — Investigative Reporters & Editors condemns President Donald Trump’s posting of a cartoon that depicts journalists being assaulted by professional fighters at the White House. The video, posted on Truth Social , undermines the role of the press in a functioning democracy. It makes light of the violence that many journalists face while simply doing their job. Last year, assaults on journalists nationwide more than doubled compared with the year before, according to the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker . IRE joins the Chauncey Bailey Project in denouncing President Trump’s juvenile and dangerous message. The Chauncey Bailey Project was established to finish the work of its namesake, the editor of the Oakland Post who was assassinated 19 years ago while walking to work. In 2023, IRE renamed its signature fellowship for journalists of color in Bailey’s honor. His death is another chapter in the sad history of violence against American journalists — a history present since IRE’s earliest days. This year, IRE is commemorating Don Bolles, an Arizona Republic reporter who was murdered 50 years ago as he worked to expose the mafia’s infiltration in the state. Many other journalists have been killed since then. In 2018, a shooter killed five employees of the Capital Gazette in Annapolis, Md., over a long-standing grudge about an article the newspaper published about him. Four years later, Las Vegas Review-Journal investigative reporter Jeff German was stabbed to death outside his home by an elected official who was angry about his reporting. Today, journalists in Washington must be able to ask questions without being intimidated by the most powerful man in political office. In addition to covering regimes that are hostile to a free press, journalists endure risks to inform the public about wars, protests and conflicts. “Journalists have a hard and at times dangerous job, but they do it because they believe in the importance of informing the public and holding the powerful to account,” said Jonathan Kealing, IRE’s executive director. “We call on the Trump administration to delete this post and refrain from posting any future videos that suggest violence against the media is an acceptable way to handle disagreements.” IRE is a grassroots nonprofit organization that seeks to improve the quality of investigative reporting. The organization began in 1975 after a small group of reporters from around the country gathered to share tips about reporting and writing. Today, it provides members access to thousands of reporting tipsheets and other materials through its Resource Center and hosts conferences and specialized training across the country.

market.title: ‘Data-informed, mission-driven’: Kyiv Independent combats war fatigue – while monetising editorial integrity
market.summary_raw: Five years after its dramatic emergence, the Kyiv Independent has solidified its status as Ukraine's premier English-language news outlet. Chief Editor Olga Rudenko reflects on the outlet’s founding, its member-funded model – and how news media can become ‘centres of gravity’ for their communities.
market.content_text: Five years ago today, the editorial team that was fired from the Kyiv Post announced it was launching a new news outlet. “We hadn’t even chosen a name,” recalls Olga Rudenko, founding chief editor of the Kyiv Independent , “but we went public on 11 November 2021, and that’s our official birthday.” They moved fast: the announcement came three days after the Post temporarily shut down. Within a week, they sent out their first newsletter and in less than two weeks, on 22 November, the first edition was launched. When full-scale war arrived three months later, the English-language startup was propelled into the global spotlight as news from and on Ukraine became paramount. “What matters to us is that we’ve grown slowly and consistently since then: in team, in subscribers, in platforms, and in the output, the offering. We’ve worked hard to turn that boost of attention into what the Kyiv Independent is now,” asserts Rudenko. Today, the Kyiv Independent is the largest English language news outlet in Ukraine, with a 36,000 subscriber base that is a mere fraction of its more than 2 million monthly readers. The outlet has been consistent in its editorial, advocacy and promotional efforts to retain and grow that base. This includes award-winning investigative reporting and, since 2023, a documentary division developed to combat war fatigue among readers, notes Rudenko. “It’s a format with a much longer shelf life, and it’s used a lot in advocacy as well. That’s our way of trying to do something with a longer and more profound impact than regular stories.” “We have to be smart about war fatigue, and we need to be reminded all the time of our mission, because the stories that matter are sometimes the ones that don’t get many clicks and aren’t popular with the audience,” explains Rudenko, referring to the outlet’s daily roundup of Russian strikes on Ukraine. This takes real reporting effort to assemble, but is least likely to be read. ”If we were driven by fatigue and the audience’s needs as we deduce them from data, we would probably slash them. We continue because they need to be there, even though fewer and fewer people want to click on them. So we need to be data-informed, but mission-driven.” Mutually beneficial membership This editorial resolve is equally evident in the Independent’s approach to its subscribers, and the role that news media can play within its communities, notes Rudenko. “We need to think of ourselves as gravity centres for our communities, not just providers of a product, which is news. That’s too narrow a way for a media outlet to define itself.” She’s a big believer in membership funding for journalism, with good reason: About 70 percent of the outlet’s 2025 revenue comes from members – and the paying base grew from 22,200 to 35,400 between September 2025 and August 2026, even as global interest in the war fell. Rudenko attributes it to two winning decisions: “Our first great decision was to start the Kyiv Independent . […]

market.title: ‘Independence isn’t declared, it’s built’: How Mediapart turned reader trust into a business model
market.summary_raw: For 18 years, French investigative outlet Mediapart has funded its journalism almost entirely through subscriptions, with no advertising, no public subsidies and no outside shareholders.
market.content_text: By Maria Lisicka “Exclusive and verified information has value, and people are okay to pay for it.” This principle has shaped Mediapart since 2008, the company’s CEO, Cécile Sourd , told participants of WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit . For Mediapart , independence has become not just an editorial value, but a legal and financial structure. In 2008, “everything was for free on the internet, including news,” Sourd recalled. Mediapart’s founders made “this crazy bet that people would actually be willing to pay for exclusive and verified information.” At first, the bet was costly: Mediapart lost money for two years, financing long investigations without enough subscribers. “It all changed when we started revealing facts that no one would have revealed if we hadn’t been there,” she explained. From then on, “people knew they could find something at Mediapart they wouldn’t read anywhere else.” “Eighteen years later, this bet paid off,” she said. Mediapart has more than 280,000 individual subscribers, who account for 99% of its annual revenue. “This is the foundation for everything else,” she said. “If your only boss is the reader, your accountability is to them only.” After reader funding, the second pillar is legal: in 2019, Mediapart created the Fonds pour une Presse Libre (Fund for a Free Press), an endowment fund that supports independent French media. Crucially, it permanently holds Mediapart’s capital, “which makes it impossible for an outside shareholder to take control of the newsroom.” The third pillar is financial sustainability. Mediapart has been profitable for 15 years, carries no loans and self-finances its investments. Together, these pillars mean “independence isn’t just a slogan, it’s a financial and legal architecture.” ‘Not above, but within society’ “Being financially independent isn’t enough,” Sourd stressed. “You also have to build a direct relationship of trust with your audience.” That starts with participation. Subscribers publish their own posts in Le Club, and Mediapart co-produced a reader-funded cinema documentary on the Sarkozy-Gaddafi affair, Personne n’y comprend rien. “The core idea is that journalism shouldn’t be above, but within, society, in a direct interaction with it.” It continues with transparency. Mediapart publishes its full annual accounts, explains its investigative methods in a section called La Boîte Noire (“The Black Box”), and asks journalists to declare their interests. “You can’t demand transparency from the powerful people you scrutinise if you don’t hold yourself to the same standards,” Sourd noted. Finally, Mediapart meets readers at free events and answers them through customer service run by real people rather than AI. […]

market.content_text: When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms. A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner : As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time. During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and new hybrid work schedules. On Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some: The Toledo Blade (Ohio) — owned by Block Communications. (Block has said it will sell or close The Blade by the end of the year.) The New York Daily News (New York) — owned by Tribune Publishing at the time; Alden acquired Tribune in 2021. Orlando Sentinel (Florida) — owned by Tribune Publishing at the time; Alden acquired Tribune in 2021. The Morning Call (Pennsylvania) — owned by Tribune Publishing; Alden acquired Tribune in 2021. Capital Gazette (Maryland) — owned by Tribune Publishing; Alden acquired Tribune in 2021. Carroll County Times (Maryland) — owned by Tribune Publishing; Alden acquired Tribune in 2021. The Patriot Ledger (Massachusetts) — owned by USA Today Co. The Enterprise (Massachusetts) — owned by USA Today Co. Milford Daily News (Massachusetts) — owned by USA Today Co. MetroWest Daily News (Massachusetts) — owned by USA Today Co. The Herald News (Massachusetts) — owned by USA Today Co. Taunton Daily Gazette (Massachusetts) — owned by USA Today Co. McDonough County Voice (Illinois) — owned by USA Today Co. The Hartford Courant (Connecticut) — owned by Alden Global Capital Are there any I’m missing? Let me know. And read the full piece here .

market.title: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.
market.summary_raw: In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.” As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that...
market.content_text: In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.” As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered. For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,” we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways. The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw. Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary. Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment. Conversational AI as a friction-reducing information intermediary Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly. “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024. We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). […]
